newsitem.title: MEXICO: Arrested Mexican says he is not guerrilla chief.
newsitem.headline: Arrested Mexican says he is not guerrilla chief.

text.p: Mexico's government claimed it had arrested a leader of a feared Marxist guerrilla group, but the suspect said on Tuesday he was not tied to the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR).

Under the headline "EPR ringleader falls" the Interior Ministry announced in a statement on Monday evening that police had arrested alleged EPR rebel chief Benigno Guzman earlier in the day at his home in Mexico City.

Officials presented the arrest as a breakthrough in the government's war against the EPR, a violent rebel group that first appeared last June. The EPR has attacked mainly army and police posts, killing more than 30 people in a bid to force out President Ernesto Zedillo's government.

But in an interview with Reuters from a jail in the tourist resort city of Acapulco, Guzman said: "I reject being linked to the Popular Revolutionary Army. The government has the old habit of whenever there is a movement, they say we'll cut off the head and be finished with all of it."

The Guzman family also issued a statement entitled "The Interior Ministry Is Lying." It said Guzman was a founder of the OCSS, a peasant organization in the state of Guerrero, which had always worked within the law.
After his arrest Guzman was charged with various offenses, including rioting, sabotage, conspiracy, robbery, and disobediance. But none of the charges contain any reference to links to the EPR.
He said that persecution of the peasant groups intensified after the massacre of 17 peasants at Aguas Blancas in Guerrero in June 1995 by members of a police motor patrol.
"After the massacre they (the government) started to persecute me and it continued on until yesterday when they decided that I should fall into their hands," Guzman said.

He said the government was trying to tie his peasant group to the armed rebels because the initial appearance of the EPR came at a meeting to commemorate the Augas Blancas killings in late June last year where peasant groups were present.
"But we were never an armed movement," he added.
Twenty unidentified armed men burst in on the Guzman home on Monday and arrested him as he was teaching his four young children to read.
He was blindfolded and taken to a car, where he was asked if he was ready to die.
"I am ready for whatever you say, and if you are going to kill me, the hour is right," Guzman said he told them.
A government spokesman said on Tuesday that other suspected EPR members had identified Guzman as a leader in confessions to the authorities.

The FAC-MLN, a hard-left umbrella group for more than 400 grassroots organizations including the OCSS, has complained that more than 200 left-wing activists throughout the country have been arrested as part of a national clampdown on suspected EPR members or sympathizers ahead of July congressional elections.

Little is known about the EPR's structure or leaders, but leading commentator Raymundo Riva Palacio wrote in a column on Monday that the authorities feared the group might carry out a big kidnapping or assassination before the elections.
